title: Looks Legit — a game about fooling lazy AI art appraisers
author: webholt
selftext:
Play free in your browser: [webholt.itch.io/looks-legit](https://webholt.itch.io/looks-legit) (also available for windows and linux).

The irony isn't lost on me: a game about fooling lazy AI was itself mostly written by an AI. Almost all the code, the dialogue and the art came out of a coding assistant. My part was the idea, the design calls, a lot of playtesting and a lot of saying "no, that's not funny, try again."

The appraisal models in the game are deliberately dumb. One sees only the average colour of an 8×8 grid, one counts colour proportions, one sees edges, one sees a light/dark silhouette. You look through each model's eyes and paint the cheapest copy it will accept. In a way the game is about what happens when you trust a narrow automated check, and I spent the whole project checking the AI's work by actually playing it.

How it was made

* *Stack*: Godot 4 and GDScript. The assistant was Claude Code (Opus 5.5).
* *Prototypes first*. Before the real project there were several throwaway prototypes: a sandbox to calibrate the four models, then three variants of the meta-game (story campaign, roguelike, smuggling routes). The AI made each one quickly, and I picked what was fun. A design doc stayed the source of truth, so the AI didn't drift from it.
* *Let the AI check its own work*. The game has a test that proves every job is solvable with the given palette and thresholds. An autoplay mode plays the whole campaign headless. Command-line flags render any screen to a PNG, so the assistant could actually look at the UI it built. That caught a lot: overlapping text, buttons sticking out, glyphs that turn into boxes in the web build.
* *Art is vector and pixel art drawn as code by the assistant, no image generators*. The paintings are simplified pixel versions of famous works with parody titles.

Happy to answer questions about the workflow.
